questions.stem: ‘He donated the library in his father's name, though the two had not spoken in twenty years.’ What motivation does this sentence most strongly imply?
options: a wish to punish his father publicly for the years of their estrangement
simple generosity toward the town, with no connection to his father
pressure from his father, who had insisted that he pay for the library
a wish to make amends, at least in public, for a broken relationship
questions.explanation: 'Though' sets the gift against the long silence, suggesting he is trying to repair or atone for the rift. The father's name on the gift rules out a motive unconnected to him, and they had not spoken, so the father could not have pressed him.

questions.stem: A character betrays a friend to the authorities, but the text reveals she did so to protect her younger brother. This revelation complicates the betrayal mainly by:
options: showing that the character was never really friends with the victim
inviting readers to weigh loyalty to family against loyalty to a friend
proving to readers that the friend fully deserved to be reported
making the younger brother, not the character herself, the text's real villain
questions.explanation: Knowing her motive turns a simple betrayal into a conflict between two loyalties, which makes judgement harder. Nothing suggests the friend deserved it; the complexity lies in the character's choice.

questions.stem: ‘“Your mother would have been proud,” her aunt said, straightening Leila's collar a little too hard.’ The detail 'a little too hard' most likely suggests:
options: the aunt's genuine and entirely uncomplicated pride in Leila
the aunt's physical frailty and her failing health in old age
that Leila's mother is standing beside them during the scene
resentment or control beneath the aunt's apparent warmth
questions.explanation: The rough gesture undercuts the kind words, hinting at tension in the relationship. 'Would have been proud' implies the mother is absent or dead, not present.

questions.stem: In a play, a father and son only ever talk while doing chores side by side, never facing each other. This staging most likely suggests:
options: open hostility that has ended all communication between the two
that the son is a servant the family employs to work on the farm
that the father cares about farm work and nothing else in his life
a closeness that is real but can only be expressed indirectly
questions.explanation: They do talk, and keep doing so, but only when their bodies are occupied and their eyes are elsewhere, which suggests intimacy that cannot be faced directly. Because they communicate, 'ended all communication' is contradicted by the staging.

questions.stem: In an analytical essay, describing a character as a 'construct' reminds the reader that:
options: the author shapes characters deliberately in order to explore ideas
every character in a text is closely based on a real person the author knew
characters always matter less to a text's meaning than its settings
the reader invents a character's traits, independent of the text
questions.explanation: Calling a character a construct shifts attention from the character as a person to the author's choices and purposes. Characters are built from the text's language, not from the reader's invention alone.

questions.stem: A novel is set almost entirely in a hospital waiting room. Which is most likely a function of this setting?
options: it offers an exotic, far-off backdrop that entertains readers with scenes of travel
it signals that the novel will move rapidly between a great many locations
it establishes that the events of the story take place in the distant past
it traps the characters together, forcing tensions into the open as they wait
questions.explanation: A confined setting where people must wait brings conflicts to the surface. A single waiting room is the opposite of an exotic or fast-changing setting.

questions.stem: In a film, the family home is lit with warm light early on, and in cold blue tones after the father leaves. The change mainly conveys:
options: that the family has moved out and now lives in a different house
that the film has jumped back in time to before he arrived
that his leaving has made the rest of the family much happier
how the family's emotional world has shifted with his absence
questions.explanation: Lighting and colour signal mood, and the shift from warm to cold mirrors loss. The setting is the same home, lit differently, so the family has not moved.

questions.stem: A novel alternates its chapters between a grandmother's wartime youth and her granddaughter's present-day life. This dual timeline most likely:
options: invites readers to compare how each generation faces similar choices
presents all of the novel's events in a strict chronological order
suggests to readers that the granddaughter is an unreliable narrator
means the two timelines need no connection to one another at all
questions.explanation: Placing two eras side by side encourages readers to look for parallels and contrasts. Alternating between past and present is, by definition, not chronological.

questions.stem: A crime novel reveals only in its final chapter that the narrator was present at the crime. On a second reading, the earlier chapters are most likely to seem:
options: full of evasions that readers first took at face value
pointless, since the ending cancels out what came before
more trustworthy, since the narrator was an eyewitness
narrated by someone else, an omniscient outside voice
questions.explanation: Knowing the narrator's involvement makes earlier gaps and deflections look deliberate, which deepens the reading. Being present at the crime gives the narrator a reason to conceal, not a claim to trust.

questions.stem: A story about a bitter divorce is told entirely by the couple's eight-year-old daughter. A key effect of this point of view is that:
options: readers gain complete and objective access to both parents' private thoughts and feelings
the narration feels distant and impersonal because it comes from outside the family
readers are told directly and explicitly which of the two parents is to blame
adult conflicts are glimpsed only in part, so readers infer more than she understands
questions.explanation: A child narrator reports what she sees without fully grasping it, so readers piece together the adult story. She is inside the family and limited, so her view is neither omniscient nor distant.

questions.stem: A novel moves between three narrators, each describing the same party differently. This structure mainly:
options: suggests that truth depends on perspective, so readers must weigh the accounts
reveals that just one narrator's account is the single correct version of events
shows that the author had not decided how the party actually unfolded
removes tension, since readers are told in advance how everything ends
questions.explanation: Conflicting accounts make readers judge each narrator's reliability and see that perspective shapes what is 'true'. The different versions are a deliberate structural choice, not indecision.

questions.stem: ‘She would not cry. Not here, not in front of them.’ The narration is in the third person, yet it captures the character's thoughts in her own idiom. This technique is:
options: a dramatic monologue
an omniscient summary
free indirect discourse
second-person narration
questions.explanation: Free indirect discourse blends a third-person narrator with a character's inner voice, as in the fragment 'Not here'. A dramatic monologue is a speech by one character to a listener, in the first person.

questions.stem: A narrative that begins 'in medias res':
options: starts in the middle of the action
starts with a detailed family history
ends at the same point where it began
is told in reverse chronological order
questions.explanation: In medias res is Latin for 'into the middle of things', describing an opening that drops readers into events. Ending where a story began describes a circular structure.

questions.stem: Early in a novel, a character jokes that the old bridge 'won't survive another flood'. Two hundred pages later, it collapses. The early line is an example of:
options: a flashback
dramatic irony
an epiphany
foreshadowing
questions.explanation: An early hint of a later event is foreshadowing, which builds anticipation. Dramatic irony requires the audience to know something the characters do not, and here no one knows the bridge will fall.

questions.stem: On stage, the audience sees a letter confessing the theft hidden in a drawer, while the accused servant pleads her innocence to a master who has not found it. The audience's position creates:
options: verbal irony, because the servant says the opposite of what she means
a soliloquy, because the servant reveals her private thoughts aloud
foreshadowing, because the scene hints at events from the servant's past
dramatic irony, heightening tension because we know more than the characters
questions.explanation: The audience knows of the confession while the master does not, which is dramatic irony. The servant is speaking sincerely to another character, so it is neither verbal irony nor a soliloquy.

questions.stem: An implicit idea in a text is one that is:
options: stated directly and plainly by the narrator or by one of the characters
found only in the author's own interviews, private notes and published letters
accepted in exactly the same way by every reader who reads the text
suggested through detail, structure or imagery rather than stated outright
questions.explanation: Implicit ideas must be inferred from patterns and choices in the text. An idea stated directly by the narrator or a character is explicit.

questions.stem: A character declares: 'Nobody gets ahead in this town without a cousin on the council.' Which idea is presented explicitly?
options: that the town is just about to hold an election for its council
that the character is related to a member of the town council
that getting ahead in the town depends on personal connections
that the character secretly admires the council and its members
questions.explanation: The character states outright that advancement depends on who you know, so the idea is explicit. Nothing indicates an election, admiration or family ties.

questions.stem: Throughout a novel, every meal the mother cooks is described in loving detail, but no one ever thanks her. An implicit idea is that:
options: the mother works as a professional chef in a restaurant
the family's gratitude is what holds the household together
women's domestic work is essential yet taken for granted
the family cannot afford enough food to eat each week
questions.explanation: The pattern of rich description and absent thanks implies the mother's labour is valued by the text but overlooked by the family. The silence of the family contradicts any idea that gratitude holds them together.

questions.stem: A soldier longs to desert but fears bringing shame on his family. This is best described as:
options: a conflict between the soldier and the natural world
a conflict already resolved in the text's exposition
an internal conflict between personal desire and duty
an external conflict between two opposing armies
questions.explanation: The struggle takes place within the soldier, between what he wants and what he feels he owes. A war between armies is an external conflict, and that is not what is described.

questions.stem: A novel is called 'The Locked Garden'. The garden, which the daughter is forbidden to enter, is opened to her in the final chapter. The garden most likely symbolises:
options: the author's own lifelong interest in plants and botany
the dangers of the natural world beyond the family home
the freedom and knowledge the daughter has been denied
the family's wealth, earned from its farming business
questions.explanation: A forbidden space that opens at the end suggests something withheld and finally granted. Nothing in the details points to wealth or danger.

questions.stem: In a film, the camera lingers in close-up on a mother's hands as she signs adoption papers. The close-up mainly:
options: shows the scene through the eyes of the baby being adopted
signals a flashback to an event from her own childhood
focuses viewers on the weight and finality of her decision
establishes the wider setting of the room where she signs
questions.explanation: A close-up isolates a detail and asks viewers to dwell on it, here the act of signing. A wide or establishing shot, not a close-up, would show the setting.

questions.stem: In a poem, a line ends 'I let go' and the next line begins 'of the rope.' The enjambment mainly:
options: slows the poem down with a full stop at the end of the line
creates a moment of ambiguity before the meaning is completed
rhymes the phrase with the final word of the following line
marks the end of a stanza and a change of speaker in the poem
questions.explanation: Running the sentence over the line break lets 'I let go' briefly suggest a wider surrender before it narrows to the rope. Enjambment means there is no end-stop at the line break.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses appropriate metalanguage to discuss an author's choices?
options: The author probably wrote it this way because she was bored at the time.
The author's fragmented structure mirrors the narrator's shattered memory.
The book is really sad and I honestly could not put it down at all.
In the book, the narrator forgets lots of things and gets very confused.
questions.explanation: 'Fragmented structure' names a text structure and links it to meaning. The other sentences give a personal reaction, retell the plot, or guess at the author's mood.

questions.stem: Analysing a text's social and cultural values means considering:
options: the sales figures, reviews and literary awards that the text has received
the number of characters in the text and how old each of them is
the author's daily writing routine while working on the text
the beliefs and attitudes of the society the text depicts or comes from
questions.explanation: Social and cultural values are the beliefs about what matters within a society, which a text may reflect, endorse or challenge. Sales and awards say nothing about those beliefs.

questions.stem: In a novel set in a 1920s country town, a woman who defies her family to study law is punished with isolation, yet the narrator presents her with sympathy. The text most likely:
options: critiques the town's values by showing what they cost her
endorses the town's view that she was wrong to defy them
shows that the 1920s placed no limits on women's careers
suggests that studying law was common for country women
questions.explanation: Her punishment reveals the town's values, and the sympathetic narration invites readers to question them. The isolation she suffers shows there were real limits on women at the time.

questions.stem: A novel written in the 1960s presents a father hitting his son as a normal part of discipline. A reader today is likely to respond differently from its first readers mainly because:
options: readers today cannot understand any text written before they were born
the novel's first readers were never its intended audience at all
attitudes to the physical punishment of children have changed since then
the words of the novel have been altered in later, modern editions
questions.explanation: The study design asks how values in a text are understood by different audiences, and readers bring their own era's values. The text has not changed; the context of reading has.

questions.stem: A narrator calls the striking workers 'the rabble' and their employer 'the old man, who had built the town from nothing'. Through this vocabulary, readers are positioned to:
options: see the narrator as a neutral and impartial observer
regard both groups as equally admirable and justified
side with the employer and view the workers with suspicion
sympathise with the workers as victims of exploitation
questions.explanation: 'Rabble' belittles the workers while the employer is credited with building the town, so the narrator's sympathies are clear. Loaded words like these show that the narrator is not neutral.

questions.stem: To argue that a text challenges a value rather than endorses it, which evidence would be strongest?
options: the value was widely held in society at the time the text was written
characters who hold the value suffer consequences the text presents as costly
the value is mentioned many times in the dialogue of several characters
the author's biography shows that she herself was raised to hold the value strongly
questions.explanation: How a text treats those who hold a value, through consequences and the narrator's stance, shows whether it questions that value. Frequent mention shows only that the value matters to the text, not which way the text leans.

questions.stem: In an analytical essay, why should a student distinguish between the author and the narrator?
options: the author and the narrator are always one and the same person in a text
narrators in fiction never express values or opinions of their own
only the author's own biography can be discussed in an analytical essay about a text
the narrator's views may differ from those the author invites readers to hold
questions.explanation: An author can create a narrator whose attitudes the text exposes or questions, so equating them can lead to misreading. Many narrators, especially first-person ones, express strong values.

questions.stem: Topic: '“The past cannot be escaped.” To what extent does the text support this view?' A strong response would most likely:
options: agree with the claim completely, as 'to what extent' requires total agreement
discuss the past in general without referring to the quoted claim
summarise the plot of the text in order from beginning to end
take a clear position on how far, and in what ways, the claim holds
questions.explanation: 'To what extent' asks for a judgement of degree, which usually means showing where the claim holds and where it falls short. It does not demand full agreement.

questions.stem: Topic: 'The novel suggests that ambition always destroys.' Discuss. Which word most invites a nuanced, qualified response?
options: suggests
ambition
always
novel
questions.explanation: Absolute words like 'always' invite a student to test the claim's limits, for example by finding ambition that does not destroy. 'Ambition' is the key concept to define, but the absolute is what opens up a qualified argument.

questions.stem: Topic: 'How does the text explore the cost of loyalty?' Which topic sentence best answers it?
options: Loyalty is when you stick by someone you care about no matter what it is that they have done.
The author was born in Hungary and moved to Adelaide as a teenager with her family.
Through Marta's silence at the trial, the author reveals that loyalty can demand self-betrayal.
In chapter six, Marta attends the trial of her younger brother and stays quiet for the whole of it.
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence makes an arguable point that answers the topic and links it to the author's choices. Retelling chapter six gives an event without an argument.

questions.stem: Which sentence best integrates evidence into analysis?
options: Kai says 'fine, honestly fine'. This is a quote that shows the reader that Kai is fine.
'Fine, honestly fine.' This quote is in the middle of the novel, on page forty-two.
Kai is not really fine at all, and the author shows this to readers in many places.
Kai's insistence that he is 'fine, honestly fine' exposes, through repetition, a fear he cannot admit.
questions.explanation: The quote is embedded in the sentence and the language feature, repetition, is linked to an insight. Asserting a point without evidence, or quoting without analysis, does neither.

questions.stem: A student's body paragraph mostly describes what happens in three scenes. The best way to revise it is to:
options: remove all quotations so the paragraph can focus more clearly on the events
replace the scenes with the student's own views on the topic
use each scene as evidence for an argument about the text's ideas
add a fourth scene so that the retelling of the plot is complete
questions.explanation: Analytical writing uses events and quotations as evidence for a point, rather than retelling them. Adding more retelling would make the paragraph's weakness worse.

questions.stem: Which plan best develops and sustains an argument across an analytical essay?
options: each paragraph advances a distinct facet of the contention, building to a nuanced conclusion
each paragraph discusses a different character, without any link back to the topic
each paragraph restates the contention using new quotes from the same single scene
each paragraph lists the text's techniques in the order in which they appear
questions.explanation: Sustaining an argument means each paragraph adds something new that develops the contention. Restating it with fresh quotes adds evidence but no development.

questions.stem: An effective conclusion to an analytical essay should:
options: apologise for any points about the text that the essay did not have time for
draw the argument together and offer a final insight into the text's ideas
introduce a new quotation and a new main point the essay has not yet covered
retell the ending of the text in detail so the reader knows how it finishes
questions.explanation: A conclusion resolves the argument and can widen it slightly, but it should not open new points. New evidence belongs in a body paragraph.

questions.stem: Which reading strategy best helps a student draw out a text's meanings on a second reading?
options: reading only the first and last chapters to save time on the text
relying on a film adaptation instead of rereading the text itself
memorising a published study guide's chapter-by-chapter summary
tracking recurring images and patterns, and noting how they shift
questions.explanation: Following patterns such as motifs across a text reveals meanings that a first reading may miss. Summaries and adaptations replace the student's own close reading.

questions.stem: When listening to a talk about a text's historical context, which cue best signals that a key point is coming?
options: a short pause while the speaker stops to take a drink of water
the speaker mentioning how many minutes remain before the session ends
the speaker thanking the audience for coming along to the talk
a discourse marker such as 'The crucial thing to understand is…'
questions.explanation: Discourse markers and stressed words are prominent cues that a speaker is about to make an important point. A pause to drink signals nothing about content.

questions.stem: In a class discussion, a peer argues that a text's ending is bleak. Which reply best tests and extends that view?
options: ‘I agree with you completely, so let's move straight on to the next text.’
‘The film version of the story had a different ending to the book anyway.’
‘That holds for the final scene, but how do you read the letter she leaves behind?’
‘You're wrong about that, because it is obviously meant to be a happy ending.’
questions.explanation: The reply accepts part of the view and tests it against new evidence, which extends the discussion. Flat disagreement without evidence shuts it down.

questions.stem: A student comparing how two texts present grief plans each paragraph around one shared idea, discussing both texts within it. This approach is called:
options: an integrated comparison
a block comparison
a text-by-text summary
a single-text analysis
questions.explanation: An integrated, or woven, comparison discusses both texts in every paragraph. A block comparison deals with one text fully and then the other.

questions.stem: In a comparative essay, why is an integrated structure usually stronger than a block structure?
options: it means the student no longer needs to analyse either text's language
it requires the student to use far fewer quotations from both texts
it keeps similarities and differences in view within every paragraph
it lets the student finish discussing one text before starting the other
questions.explanation: Discussing both texts together forces direct comparison throughout, rather than leaving it to the conclusion. Finishing one text before starting the other describes a block structure.
